children: NBFCs tighten rural lending in drought-hit districts as weakening farm incomes and rising delinquencies increase credit risks and threaten asset quality in FY27

Several non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) have tightened underwriting standards and calibrated loan disbursements in drought-affected districts across Maharashtra, Karnataka and Telangana as emerging rural repayment stress threatens loan growth and asset quality in the second half of FY27.

Although the sector reported strong growth during the September quarter, lenders are increasingly monitoring early-stage delinquencies and stressed portfolios, particularly in agricultural and rural-linked financing. Farm equipment, commercial vehicles, construction equipment and microfinance are among the segments facing heightened risks.
Rural Stress Pushes Lenders Towards Cautious Underwriting

Vehicle financiers reported credit costs of around 2 per cent in Q2FY27, compared with 1.8 per cent in the preceding quarter. Early delinquencies also increased at select lenders, including Shriram Finance, amid weakening rural cash flows and lower agricultural activity.

Disbursement growth among vehicle financiers accelerated to 31 per cent year-on-year during the September quarter, against 21 per cent in the preceding quarter. However, analysts expect lending momentum to moderate in the second half as weaker rural incomes and a high base weigh on demand. The stress is particularly visible in drought-affected locations where lower farm output can reduce household earnings, weaken consumption and stretch repayment capacity.
Microfinance Credit Costs Rise Despite Better Asset Quality

NBFC-microfinance institutions reported an improvement in gross Stage-3 assets, which declined to 2.3 per cent in Q2FY27 from 2.8 per cent in the previous quarter. However, credit costs increased to 3.7 per cent from 3.2 per cent, reflecting emerging repayment pressure. CreditAccess Grameen reported an increase in Stage-2 assets and portfolio-at-risk beyond 15 days amid drought-related stress in Maharashtra, which accounts for around 22 per cent of its assets under management.
Growth Remains Strong but Profitability Risks Persist

Despite rural stress, the 23 NBFCs tracked by JM Financial reported 21 per cent year-on-year AUM growth in Q2FY27, while profit after tax increased around 40 per cent. Net interest income rose 26 per cent, supported by operating performance and broadly stable provisions.

However, higher funding costs, sticky early delinquencies and proposed changes to insurance commissions could weigh on profitability. Housing finance companies have raised lending rates by 10–25 basis points between October and November to pass on higher borrowing costs. The emerging rural stress is expected to remain a key monitorable for NBFCs in the second half of FY27, particularly as lenders balance growth ambitions with tighter underwriting and asset-quality protection.
